questions.question: What does AER stand for on a savings account?
questions.explanation: AER shows what you'd earn over a year, including compounding.

questions.question: Why use AER to compare savings accounts?
options: It includes compounding, so accounts compare fairly
questions.explanation: AER puts accounts with different interest payment schedules on a level footing.

questions.question: Easy-access vs fixed-term savings: what's the usual trade-off?
options: Fixed usually pays more but locks your money away
questions.explanation: Fixed-term accounts often pay more in exchange for tying your money up.

questions.question: Account A pays 5% on the first £1,000 and 1% on the rest. Account B pays 4% on everything. With £5,000 for a year, which earns more?
questions.explanation: A: £50 + £40 = £90. B: £200. The headline rate isn't the whole story.

questions.question: A regular saver account typically…
options: Lets you pay in a limited amount each month at a higher rate
questions.explanation: Regular savers cap monthly deposits, often with a higher rate.

questions.question: A regular saver pays 6% AER. You pay in £200 a month for 12 months. Roughly how much interest do you earn?
questions.explanation: 6% of the final £2,400 is £144, but the money isn't all there for the whole year. Your average balance is about £1,300, so you earn roughly £78.

questions.question: What is an emergency fund?
options: Money set aside for surprises like a broken boiler or job loss
questions.explanation: It's a cash buffer so surprises don't push you into debt.

questions.question: A common guideline for an emergency fund is…
questions.explanation: Many guides suggest 3–6 months of essential costs, built up gradually.

questions.question: The FSCS protects eligible savings per person, per…
questions.explanation: Protection works per banking licence, so brands sharing a licence share one limit.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT protected by the FSCS?
options: A current account at a UK-authorised bank
Money held on a crypto exchange
questions.explanation: Crypto isn't FSCS protected.

questions.question: Two bank brands share one banking licence and you have savings in both. Under the FSCS…
options: They share a single protection limit
questions.explanation: Check which brands share a licence before spreading large sums around.

questions.question: Instead of interest, Premium Bonds give you…
questions.explanation: Each £1 bond is entered into a monthly prize draw.

questions.question: Premium Bonds are backed by…
questions.explanation: NS&I is backed by HM Treasury.

questions.question: Premium Bond prizes are…
questions.explanation: Prizes are tax-free.

questions.question: Interest earned in a Cash ISA is…
questions.explanation: ISA interest is tax-free.

questions.question: How much can you pay into ISAs in total in the 2026/27 tax year?
questions.explanation: The overall ISA allowance is £20,000, split across your ISAs however you like.
questions.verify: Overall ISA allowance and any Cash ISA limit changes on gov.uk

questions.question: You take £1,000 out of a standard (non-flexible) Cash ISA, then put it back in the same tax year. What happens?
options: Putting it back uses up more of your allowance
questions.explanation: With a non-flexible ISA, money paid back counts as a new subscription. Flexible ISAs work differently.

questions.question: Inflation is 4% and your savings earn 2%. In real terms your money is…
options: Losing about 2% of its buying power a year
questions.explanation: Prices are rising faster than your interest.

questions.question: Same gross rate: interest paid monthly vs annually. Which grows slightly more if you leave the interest in?
questions.explanation: Monthly interest starts earning interest sooner, so it grows slightly more.

questions.question: AER stands for:
questions.explanation: AER lets you compare accounts fairly because it includes the effect of interest being paid more often than yearly.

questions.question: Compound interest means:
options: Interest only on your original deposit
Interest earned on your interest as well, so savings grow faster over time
questions.explanation: Compounding is what makes long-term saving powerful: growth builds on growth.

questions.question: An easy access savings account lets you:
questions.explanation: Easy access accounts trade a lower rate for full flexibility.

questions.question: Fixed-rate savings bonds typically offer:
options: Higher rates because you lock your money for a set term
questions.explanation: Fixing your money for a term usually buys a better rate, at the cost of flexibility.

questions.question: A regular saver account usually requires:
options: Monthly deposits, often capped, usually for 12 months at a higher rate
questions.explanation: Regular savers reward consistent monthly deposits with some of the best rates around.

questions.question: If inflation is higher than your savings rate, in real terms your money is:
questions.explanation: Real return = rate minus inflation. Below-inflation rates mean your cash buys less over time.

questions.question: The ISA allowance means each tax year you can save or invest tax-efficiently up to:
questions.explanation: The annual ISA allowance is £20,000 per person per tax year (this figure can change).

questions.question: Money inside a Stocks & Shares ISA:
options: Grows free of tax on gains and income, but its value can still go down
questions.explanation: The ISA wrapper shields returns from tax; it doesn't protect you from market falls.

questions.question: A Lifetime ISA (LISA) offers:
options: A 25% government bonus on up to £4,000 saved each year, for first homes or retirement
questions.explanation: LISAs add 25% to deposits up to £4,000/year, but non-qualifying withdrawals lose 25%, which is more than the bonus you got.

questions.question: Withdrawing from a LISA before 60 or without buying a first home normally costs:
options: A 25% charge on the withdrawal, so you can end up with less than you paid in
questions.explanation: The 25% charge exceeds the 25% bonus in real terms, roughly a 6.25% net loss.

questions.question: Premium Bonds:
options: Enter your savings in a monthly prize draw instead of paying interest, and you can get your money back
questions.explanation: Premium Bonds are NS&I savings with prize-draw odds instead of interest; returns are not guaranteed.

questions.question: With Premium Bonds, the maximum you can hold and the minimum buy-in are:
questions.explanation: Premium Bonds run from £25 to a £50,000 holding limit per person.

questions.question: How much emergency fund do most experts suggest for an adult with steady income?
options: One to three months of essential spending
questions.explanation: One to three months of essentials is the common starting target; more if income is unstable.

questions.question: An emergency fund should be kept:
options: Somewhere safe and instantly accessible, like an easy access account
questions.explanation: Emergencies need instant access and capital safety, not maximum growth.

questions.question: The FSCS protects eligible savings up to:
options: £85,000 per person, per authorised bank or building society
questions.explanation: The FSCS limit is £85,000 per person per authorised firm; this cap can change.

questions.question: A couple with a joint savings account is typically FSCS-protected up to:
options: £170,000 for the joint account, as £85,000 each
questions.explanation: Joint accounts usually get double protection since each holder counts for £85,000.

questions.question: You have £150,000 and want full FSCS cover. The standard approach is:
options: Put it all in one bank
Spread it across different authorised banks so no single one holds over the limit
Put it in a current account
questions.explanation: Splitting across different authorised institutions keeps every pound within the protection cap.

questions.question: A notice account requires:
options: You give advance notice, often 30-120 days, before withdrawing
questions.explanation: Notice accounts pay more than instant access in exchange for waiting out the notice period.

questions.question: Interest on UK savings is paid to you by most banks:
options: Gross, without tax deducted; you may owe tax yourself only if you exceed your personal savings allowance
questions.explanation: Banks pay interest gross; you only pay tax above your personal savings allowance, which depends on your income tax band.

questions.question: Chasing the top savings rate matters most when:
options: You have larger balances, where each 1% of rate is real money
questions.explanation: On £10,000, moving from 1% to 4% is £300 a year for an hour of admin.

questions.question: Best use of a windfall like a bonus or gift:
options: Park it in savings while you decide, so the choice isn't rushed
questions.explanation: Decide calmly; a temporary home in easy access beats rushed decisions.

questions.question: Which habit builds savings most reliably?
options: Saving whatever is left at month end
Paying yourself first: moving savings out on payday before spending
questions.explanation: Automating savings on payday makes it the default, not the leftover.

questions.question: A children's Junior ISA allowance is:
questions.explanation: Junior ISAs have their own annual allowance, separate from the adult £20,000.

questions.question: Round-up apps that save your card change work because:
options: Small automatic amounts add up without you noticing
questions.explanation: Automating micro-savings removes the willpower problem entirely.

questions.question: Before you start investing seriously, you should first have:
options: An emergency fund and expensive debt paid off
questions.explanation: Investing while carrying 25% APR debt or with no buffer usually loses on balance.

questions.question: Fixed-rate bond, withdraw early:
options: Usually means losing interest or a charge, depending on the provider's terms
questions.explanation: Read the early-access terms before locking money away; some allow none at all.

questions.question: The personal savings allowance for a basic-rate taxpayer lets you earn interest up to:
questions.explanation: Basic-rate taxpayers can earn £1,000 of savings interest tax-free; higher-rate gets £500 (figures can change).

questions.question: Savings rates quoted 'gross' and 'AER' differ when:
options: Interest is paid more often than yearly, like monthly
questions.explanation: AER smooths monthly-paid interest into an annual figure so comparisons are honest.
